{{use mdy dates|date=July 2025}}
'''Thomas Frederick Storer''' (1938 – November 9, 2006) was a [[Navajo]] American [[mathematician]] who studied [[combinatorics]] and [[cyclotomy]]. He was a [[professor]] at the [[University of Michigan]], and was one of the first Native Americans to become a PhD mathematician. In addition to his mathematical research, teaching, and mentoring, Storer also did notable work on [[string figures]].

==Education and career==
Storer, a citizen of the [[Navajo Nation]], was born in 1938.<ref name="heartseq">{{cite book|title=String Figures as Mathematics? An Anthropological Approach to String Figure-making in Oral Tradition Societies|last=Vandendriessche|chapter=Thomas Storer and the Concept of Heart-Sequence|first=Eric|series=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science| volume=36|year=2015|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-319-11993-9|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-11994-6}}</ref> He attended the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] for his bachelors degree, with the help of a [[football scholarship]].<ref name="aaobit">{{cite news|url=https://obits.mlive.com/us/obituaries/annarbor/name/thomas-storer-obituary?id=13721424|title= Thomas F. Storer Ph.D. (obituary)|via=Legacy.com|newspaper=Ann Arbor News|date=November 12, 2006|access-date=July 20, 2025}}</ref><ref name="isfatribute"/> He went on to the [[University of Southern California]] for his graduate work, receiving an MA in 1962, and a PhD in 1964.<ref name="aaobit"/><ref name="mgp">{{mathgenealogy|id=9006|name=Thomas Frederick Storer}}</ref> His thesis was titled ''A Family of Generalized Difference Sets'', and was advised by Albert Whiteman.<ref name="mgp"/> Storer was one of the first [[Native Americans]] to complete a PhD in mathematics; [[Native Hawaiian]] [[Edwin Mookini]] completed his PhD in the same year.<ref name="heartseq"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://indigenousmathematicians.org/profiles/|work=Indigenous Mathematicians|title=Doctorates in Mathematics|access-date=July 21, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202204/rnoti-p513.pdf|title=Indigenous Peoples Exist Within Mathematics|last=Yong|first=Kamuela E.|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|department=A Word From...|year=2022|volume=69|issue=4|access-date=July 30, 2025}}</ref>

In 1965, after a short period in residence in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/thomas-f-storer|title=Thomas F. Storer|publisher=Institute for Advanced Study|access-date=July 22, 2025}}</ref> Storer went to the University of Michigan, where he remained for the rest of his career.<ref name="continuum2002">{{cite news|publisher=University of Michigan|department=Department of Mathematics|newspaper=ContinuUM|title=Tom Storer Retires|url=https://lsa.umich.edu/content/dam/math-assets/math-document/continuum/summer2002.pdf|access-date=July 21, 2025|year=2002}}</ref> He was promoted to full professor in 1979, and retired to [[emeritus]] status in 2001.<ref name="isfatribute">{{cite journal|journal=Bulletin of the International String Figure Association|volume=14|pages=1–37|year=2007|title=Someone who Loved the String: a tribute to Tom Storer|last=Sherman|first=Mark|author-link=Mark Sherman (collector)}}</ref><ref name="recordobit">{{cite news|url=https://record.umich.edu/articles/obituaries-120/|title=Thomas Storer (obituary)|publisher=University of Michigan|newspaper=The University Record|date=January 8, 2007}}</ref>

At the University of Michigan, Storer was known as a teacher and mentor. In 1985, he received the Amoco Foundation Good Teaching Award.<ref name="recordobit"/> Storer was an advocate for Native American causes on the University of Michigan campus, and learned the [[Ojibwe language|language]] spoken by the [[Ojibwe people]] in Michigan.<ref name="isfatribute"/><ref name="recordobit"/> Ten doctoral students completed their PhDs with Storer as their thesis advisor, including [[Peyton Young]] (co-advised with [[Jack Edmonds]]).<ref name="mgp"/>

==String figures==
Storer also wrote several works on string figures, the designs formed by manipulating string around one's fingers. His bibliography on the topic went through three editions.<ref name="isfatribute"/> He also wrote a monograph on string figures, which appeared as a two-volume special issue of the ''[[International String Figure Association|Bulletin of String Figures Association]]''.<ref name="heartseq"/> 

{{Gallery|title=Two figures from Storer's 1988 monograph | noborder=yes | mode=nolines | width=350 
|File:Osage Diamonds schema (fig 28).pdf
| Schema representing the Osage Diamonds string figure in Storer's notation
|File:Osage Diamonds, Seifert surface (fig B.6).pdf
| [[Seifert surface]] associated with the Osage Diamonds string figure
}}

In his monograph, he devised a [[notation system]] for compactly and precisely describing string figures.<ref name="heartseq"/> The International String Figure Association began recommending that contributors use either the older notation of [[Alfred Cort Haddon|Haddon]] and [[W. H. R. Rivers|Rivers]], or else a modified, more verbose version of Storer's notation.<ref name="hoenigman">{{cite journal|journal=Language Documentation & Conservation|title=Talking about strings: The language of string figure-making in a Sepik society in Papua New Guinea | url=http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24964 |last=Hoenigman|first=Darja|volume=14|year=2020|pages=598–641}}</ref>

[[File: Osage Two Diamonds Jayne Fig 56.jpg |thumb|Osage 2-Diamonds string figure]]
For example, Storer's monograph encodes the sequence of steps for making the Osage 2-Diamonds string figure (pictured) as follows:<ref name="monograph">{{cite journal|title=String Figures|last=Storer|first=T.|date=1988|journal=Bulletin of String Figures Association|volume=16|issue=Supplemental Issue in Two Parts| pages=410 pages |publisher=Nippon Ayatori Kyokai}}</ref>{{rp|84}} 
<!-- split into several math envs to allow line-breaking --> {{hanging indent|
<math>\underline{O}.A : \square1 \vert </math> <math>\star \overrightarrow{1} (\underline{5f}) \# \vert </math> <math> \overrightarrow{1}(2n) \# N1 \vert </math> <math> \overleftarrow{2} \downarrow (1-\text{⧌}) : <2 (\#) : \square 5 \vert </math> <math> (\text{palms away)}.</math>}}

Here, the fingers are encoded with the numerals 1 through 5, with 1 representing the thumb and 5 representing the little finger.  The notation describes a sequence of movements of a loop held by one finger (a "functor", written before a set of parentheses), relative to a loop held by another finger (an "object", written inside parentheses).  The symbol <math>\square</math> denotes releasing a loop of string, while the vertical line <math>\vert</math> denotes moving hands apart so that the string is not [[Tension (physics) | slack]].<ref name="heartseq"/><ref name="monograph" />{{rp|1—28}}
{{clear}}

==Personal life==
Storer was married to Karen Storer for a period of over 30 years. They had two daughters.<ref name="isfatribute"/><ref name="recordobit"/> Storer died on November 9, 2006.<ref name="aaobit"/><ref name="recordobit"/>
